case_info.explanation: B. Obtain digital subtraction angiography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that a stroke in a young patient with bilateral narrowing of the terminal portion of the intracranial carotid arteries and a family history of stroke is highly suggestive of moyamoya disease. Intravenous heparin (choice A) is contraindicated because anticoagulation increases the risk of cerebral hemorrhage in patients with moyamoya disease. Lumbar puncture (choice C) is not recommended because there are no clinical signs of infection. Choice D is not indicated because steroids are not effective treatment for moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease is a noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disorder characterized by progressive stenosis of the terminal internal carotid artery (ICA), leading to fragile collateral vessel formation.1﻿Moyamoya(Japanese for “puff of smoke”) refers to the angiographic findings of this abnormal vascular network.2 Moyamoya disease occurs in 0.1 per 100 000 people worldwide, but the prevalence is substantially higher in East Asia, especially Japan (17.6 per 100 000).3Moyamoya disease is approximately 2-fold more common among females than males and has a bimodal age distribution (at 10 years and 30 to 50 years).4A family history of moyamoya disease is reported in 12% to 15% of patients with the disease.3 Underlying pathophysiological mechanisms are unknown but may involve alterations in genes involved in vascular development and angiogenesis, includingMMP,VEGF, andPDGFRB. TheRNF213p.R4810K gene variant increases the risk of moyamoya disease among East Asian patients.4 Patients with moyamoya disease may have intermittent transient ischemic attacks and strokes typically involving border zone areas or have hemorrhagic events (intracranial or intraventricular) due to rupture of fragile reticular vessels. Headaches affect 20% to 76.4% of patients, often with migraine-like features such as unilaterality and aura.5The differential diagnosis includes atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease, autoimmune conditions (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome), and infectious vasculopathies (eg, meningitis, cytomegalovirus infection). The diagnosis of moyamoya disease is made based on digital subtraction angiographic findings of (1) stenosis or occlusion of arteries in the terminal portion of the intracranial ICA and (2) abnormal vascular networks in the vicinity of the stenotic lesions. Brain MRI or MRA are less accurate for diagnosis, particularly in patients with unilateral lesions, those older than 60 years, or those with early-stage moyamoya disease.6 There is no curative treatment for moyamoya disease. Among patients presenting with ischemic events, surgical revascularization with a direct bypass (extracranial-intracranial anastomosis) or indirect bypass (eg, placement of superficial temporal artery onto the brain surface to promote new blood vessel growth) is associated with decreased risk of ischemic stroke and death. Patients receiving nonsurgical management of ischemic events have recurrent annual stroke rates of 20% to 50%.7 Asymptomatic patients with moyamoya disease have a 1.4% to 15% annual risk of stroke.7,8For these patients, bypass surgery is associated with a 26% reduction in the risk of death but a 76% increase in the risk of hemorrhagic events compared with nonsurgical management.7 Per 2021 Japanese guidelines, based on limited evidence (grade C), antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel, or cilostazol) can be considered to reduce the risk of stroke in patients with moyamoya disease and a history of ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, those awaiting surgery, or those ineligible for surgery due to advanced age or comorbidities.9Endovascular treatment (angioplasty and/or stent) is associated with restenosis rates of 68.8%, and high rates (9.5%) of complications such as vessel rupture and intracerebral hemorrhage.10 Digital subtraction angiography revealed an abnormal net-like vascular network with a “smoke puff” appearance near the stenotic terminal portion of the ICA bilaterally (Figure 2and video). The patient received aspirin (75 mg) and clopidogrel (75 mg). Seven days after initial presentation, she developed a new stroke and underwent an indirect bypass revascularization procedure. On postoperative day 21, she developed a right MCA ischemic stroke causing left hemiplegia. Two years later, she developed right-sided hemiparesis due to occlusion of the first segment of the left MCA and underwent direct bypass connecting the left superficial temporal artery to the left MCA. Four years after initial presentation, she has persistent left hemiparesis and a left steppage gait. Genetic testing revealed no pathogenic variants.
